justifications.functional_suitability: Catalog Service with Amazon OpenSearch handles search (R-01); Order & Checkout Service and Stripe/PayPal handle checkout (R-02); Review Service supports ratings (R-03); Recommendation Service provides co-purchase recommendations (R-04). However, dedicated mechanisms for electronic book fulfillment or digital delivery are omitted.
justifications.performance_efficiency: Edge caching via Edge Content Delivery Network (CloudFront), code splitting in React Single Page Application, ElastiCache Redis caching, and DynamoDB Global Tables effectively guarantee 1 M MAU scalability and under 2-second page loads on 3G.
justifications.compatibility: The architecture explicitly defines integration mechanisms with external systems: Fulfillment Integration connects to FedEx/UPS, Payment Orchestration integrates with Stripe/PayPal, Dispatch Adapter binds to SendGrid/SES, and Pricing & Localization Interceptor connects with Fixer exchange rate APIs.
justifications.usability: React Single Page Application covers end-user shopping, search, and checkout flows well. However, dedicated interfaces, consoles, or operational workflows for internal Administrators identified in the brief are completely absent.
justifications.reliability: High availability (99.95%) is addressed via DNS Router geo-failover, DynamoDB Global Table Replica Manager across all three AWS regions, Aurora multi-region storage, SQS Dead Letter Queues, and Fallback & Resiliency Manager in Recommendation Service.
justifications.security: AWS WAF provides explicit OWASP Top-10 mitigations, Amazon API Gateway enforces JWT auth with AWS Cognito, mTLS is mandated via AWS App Mesh, and AWS KMS encrypts sensitive data across Aurora, DynamoDB, and Compliance Audit Logger.
justifications.maintainability: System decomposition is cleanly partitioned into microservices (Catalog Service, Order & Checkout Service, Review Service) communicating via gRPC/App Mesh and asynchronous SQS events, with modular frontend components (Catalog & Search Module, Cart & Checkout Flow).
justifications.portability: The design deploys cleanly across the required AWS regions (us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1). However, extensive coupling to proprietary AWS primitives (DynamoDB, App Mesh, Kinesis, CloudFront, Route 53) restricts replaceability and cloud portability.

PERF-01.justification: CloudFront edge caching, Redis catalog caching, and DynamoDB auto-scaling absorb traffic spikes, allowing catalog and product pages to be served quickly within the 2-second target.
sensitivity_points: Cache hit ratio at CloudFront and ElastiCache Redis layers
Read throughput provisioning on DynamoDB Global Tables
tradeoffs: Aggressive edge caching increases risk of briefly stale catalog inventory data

PERF-02.justification: Pre-computed recommendation vectors stored in Redis decouple asynchronous model recomputation from synchronous catalog browsing, preventing background ML loads from degrading user response times.
sensitivity_points: Separation of compute-intensive ML training from Redis read replicas
tradeoffs: Precomputing recommendation vectors conserves real-time latency at the cost of eventual consistency

AVAIL-01.justification: The transactional outbox pattern combined with Amazon SQS buffers shipping events asynchronously, ensuring checkout succeeds without synchronous dependency on external carrier availability.
sensitivity_points: Reliability of Outbox polling and Amazon SQS message delivery
tradeoffs: Asynchronous fulfillment improves checkout availability but delays shipping label confirmation to customers

AVAIL-02.justification: Route 53 geo-DNS and DynamoDB Global Tables handle multi-region failover, but cross-region promotion of Aurora PostgreSQL writer replicas introduces slight failover latency and operational recovery overhead.
sensitivity_points: Replication lag and promotion time of Aurora cross-region read replicas
tradeoffs: Active-passive database replication maintains strict ACID integrity but adds promotion RTO during regional outages

MOD-01.justification: The Pricing & Localization Interceptor encapsulates currency conversions using external exchange rate feeds, while Stripe and PayPal natively support multi-currency checkout without widespread core architectural changes.
sensitivity_points: Abstraction level of currency formatting and conversion interceptors
tradeoffs: Centralizing exchange rate fetching simplifies currency additions but requires reliable external provider connectivity

MOD-02.justification: The Recommendation Engine is encapsulated behind a gRPC API controller and an ElastiCache Redis cache layer, allowing algorithm updates without modifying external clients or services.
sensitivity_points: Stability of internal gRPC contracts between API Controller and Engine
tradeoffs: Microservice decoupling isolates algorithmic iterations but requires maintaining internal gRPC interfaces

SEC-01.justification: AWS WAF filters malicious payloads at the edge, while API Gateway validation and parameterized database persistence components block SQLi and XSS across catalogue and review paths.
sensitivity_points: Regular updating of AWS WAF managed rule sets against OWASP Top-10
tradeoffs: Deep payload inspection at edge WAF ensures security but introduces sub-millisecond edge latency

SEC-02.justification: The Customer Privacy/Compliance Service coordinates a distributed saga via Amazon SQS to erase personal records across databases and Redis caches, logging immutable compliance records in DynamoDB.
sensitivity_points: Complete saga event consumption by all services containing personal user data
tradeoffs: Asynchronous deletion sagas ensure multi-service data consistency but require complex rollback error handling
